utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Could you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Andrew Cayley, for the Prosecution, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I'm John Ackerman. I'm with Marela Jevtovic, on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I have to ask the accused, can they follow the proceedings in a language they understand?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, my name is Natasha Fauveau-Ivanovic, on behalf of General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, the accused, can they follow the proceedings in a language they understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. There is something wrong with my headphones and I cannot follow; I cannot hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me for a moment. You may not have heard General Talic. He said that he could not hear. I guess he can hear now. It guess it's been fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I had the impression that it was fixed and I saw from the reaction that it was functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am sorry. I'm very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Everybody can follow the proceedings. So the issue of this morning's session is only the motion of 25 April, 2002 to qualify the Trial Chamber hearing the Brdjanin Talic trial. Such a motion is a very serious issue, of course. To a certain extent, it may endanger the continuity of the ongoing trial. In any event, it threatens the necessary atmosphere of mutual trust in the courtroom. Evidently, such a motion is a signal that one party has, to a certain extent, lost confidence in this common spirit of cooperation necessary also and especially in adversarial procedure. Therefore, it demands immediate reaction in order to come back to proceed to next business as soon as possible, whatever the outcome of this procedure will be. Though this procedure is a very formal one, I want to give them general remarks in the beginning. I would invite the parties to show throughout the discussion of this motion the necessary self-restraint, even though the matter before us may invite for a possible discussion cum ira et studio, with zeal and fury, whereas lawyers always should act sine ira et studio, without zeal and fury. This is especially true and here I want once again appeal to you in an International Tribunal. The Judges of this International Tribunal and also, to a certain extent, the participants in such a trial, are not only mandated to hear the trial in a criminal court, but what we are doing here is at the same time a peace-keeping mission, and we should bear this in mind also when dealing with issues with very sensitive issues as it was brought before us today. I want in this context to quote from Security Council Resolution 827 of 1993, Kofi Annan saying, "This Tribunal has to contribute to the restoration and maintenance of peace." And from my point of view this has also an impact on our behaviour, on our attitude to these criminal proceedings. Having a lot of experience for all sides of the Bench, as an acting Defence counsel, as an acting Prosecutor, I know very well that it doesn't help to put things just under the carpet to come as close as possible to harmony. This is not the point. The point is that we should try to be fair to each other, to be fair to each other in a very special environment, a special environment because we should always take into account that we have to bring together totally different legal traditions: Legal traditions of the civil law system and the common law system. Some Judges have a more diplomat background, some have a more criminal law background. To come from this from outside, it is sometimes really difficult to understand the other system, and this may cause some difficulty of understanding. To give you an example, something you can identify in the Rules, for example, the request to have a kind of judgment after the hearing of the Prosecutor's case would be impossible in some legal systems. And this would be a reason for calling Judges biased. Other issues you have to be aware of in this Tribunal sometimes are really surprising for a judge, a lawyer coming from a civil law system: Not to have contacts directly with the Judge, not to have contacts directly with the Prosecutor, going through legal officers, and so on. This causes additional problems and this is why -- and I am quite sure you are aware of all the former decisions on this qualification of Judges, be it decisions as such, be the threshold given in other judgments, that this threshold here is a very high one. We came together today under Rule 15(B). On purpose, I quote: "Any party may apply to the Presiding Judge of a Chamber for the disqualification and withdrawal of a Judge of that Chamber from a trial or appeal upon the above grounds. The Presiding Judge shall confer with the Judge in question, and if necessary the Bureau shall determine the matter. If the Bureau upholds the application, the President will assign another Judge to sit in place of the disqualified Judge." Already here, and therefore I quoted it. In other legal systems, one could come to the conclusion that the motion as it is before us is obviously inadmissible because it is on the disqualification of the Trial Chamber. And for example, in my judicial system, such a motion would be rejected immediately because it is not on the individual, let's call it "misbehaviour," alleged misbehaviour of a single Judge or of three Judges. But you never can't challenge a Chamber in my system, just to show you the different approaches in different legal systems. Having said this, of course, I don't want to say that this motion is not admissible. I only wanted to point out here that we have different approaches. 15(B) leaves us alone, to a certain extent, on the question how to proceed. Of course, the presiding Judge shall confer with the Judge in question, and this I did. I formally summoned the three Judges and I report on the outcome of this immediately. There is nothing about a hearing, but I personally read the Rules always in the view of the human rights, especially the European Convention of Human Rights, and therefore I regard it necessary, having conferred with the Judges in question, to inform you on that because this forms part of the right to be heard before a decision. And as you may see, it is open for discussion. The Rules provide that possibly the presiding Judge can decide, and if he regards it necessary, he can transfer the case to the Bureau. This was the reason why I invited you on yesterday's first decision to a hearing in application of 65 ter (I) correspondingly. But I learned that it was the wish of both parties to have a hearing in public, and I appreciate it, especially in a Tribunal working in a system of total transparency. Therefore, we have come together and we should discuss the issues before us. The issue is limited by the motion before us and I invite the parties, once again, also here to show self-restraint and not to go over this limit given by the motion from 25 April, 2002. To come to a certain order, additionally, I want to invite the parties first to address factual questions, and later on, legal questions on the basis of former decisions of the Tribunal on disqualification of Judges. Proceeding now, I want to tell you what was the outcome of the conference with the challenged Judges and, therefore, may I ask the usher to distribute the minutes of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy, Your Honour, please? Could the interpreters have a copy of the document, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the record, I want to read out the minutes of this meeting convened this 26th of April, 8.30, on the basis of an order given yesterday. The document reads: "Minutes of the meeting Judge Schomburg held with the Judges Agius, Janu and Taya on the motion for disqualification of the Bench submitted for the Defence of Brdjanin and Talic. 1. The three Judges were aware that the pre-municipality meeting was scheduled for 25 April, 2002, chaired by senior legal officer. 2. Judges Janu and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the President slow down, please, for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 3. Judges Janu and Taya had not been informed by their own staff of the agenda of that meeting. 4. Judges Janu and Taya had never seen the list of potential agreed facts prior to the pre-municipality meeting. The Bench at no point prior to the pre-municipality meeting discussed the agenda of that meeting. 6. The Bench at no point prior to the pre-municipality meeting discussed the question of whether draft agreed facts should be presented and at no point discussed the list distributed. 7. Judge Agius knew that the legal staff working on this case had prepared an agenda for this meeting and knew the issues to be discussed. 8. Judge Agius instructed the staff to consult with parties through this pre-municipality meeting to try to identify with the parties facts on which they could possibly agree. This would possibly avoid witnesses to testify upon such facts. 9. Judge Agius consulted prior to the pre-municipality meeting with the senior legal officer about the pre-municipality meeting. During this meeting, the focus was on methods to speed up the trial as much as possible. 10. Judge Agius knew that there was a list prepared. 11. Judge Agius was not involved in the drafting of the list. 12. Judge Agius never saw the distributed list prior to the pre-municipality meeting but was aware that it was distributed amongst parties one day before the pre-municipality meeting by the legal staff. 13. Judge Agius was provided a memo on the pre-municipality meeting one day before that meeting. That memo included also a possible list of agreed facts but was not identical to the one distributed to the parties. Inter alia the heading of the document distributed did not appear in the memo provided to Judge Agius. 14. If Judge Agius would have seen the document prior to its distribution, he would not have agreed with certain parts of the text. The parts he would not have agreed upon include inter alia the introduction to the list, the paragraph on the criminal responsibility of the accused, the paragraph on the composition of the population of Sanski Most in 1995, and the paragraph stating that Manjaca camp belonged to the 1st Krajina Corps. 15. Also, Judges Janu and Taya would not have agreed to this version of the list being distributed. So far the report on the meeting based on Rule 15(B) of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence. I would now invite first the moving party to address in short and in the limits of their own motion first the factual and then legal aspects of this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may begin on behalf of Mr. Brdjanin, if that is agreeable with you. I have listened carefully to your opening remarks, Your Honour, and I appreciate them, and to a great extent, I accept and adopt and agree with them. I want to begin with what you have just presented us, and that is the minutes of your meeting with the Judges, and I will say that the results of that meeting confirm what I had initially suspected to be the facts and reality of this situation. I have a statement prepared, Your Honour, that was -- that is a joint statement on behalf of both parties, and I hope that you will see it as following the guidelines that you have set down this morning. Yesterday, Your Honour, I had occasion to speak upon this matter several times, both formally and informally. With the exception of every Defence lawyer here who understood it without exception, I had the definite feeling that I was not being understood. That can only be my fault and I must therefore try again. First, I must say that I fully accept the statement of Judge Agius made in open court yesterday on behalf of himself and the Judges Janu and Taya. I accept completely and understand that a Trial Chamber has the right, and perhaps even the duty, to attempt to get the parties to come to agreement regarding facts in the case as to which there is no reasonable dispute. Some believe that my challenge was that the Chamber did not have that right. That is not the case, and I do not challenge that aspect of this matter. On April 24th, we were handed a document which in its preamble told us two things: One, the Chamber had asked the Prosecutor for a list of facts that the parties can agree on or do not contest. It appears from the document that this was an ex parte communication. Whether ex parte or not, it is in my mind an improper communication. On the other hand, a letter to all parties in which the Prosecutor is asked to supply a list of facts to the Defence as a possible basis for agreement and discussion is wholly appropriate and fully accomplishes the apparent intent of the Trial Chamber. It would have developed, Your Honour, that in the course of this case, such agreements would have been forthcoming. I must say to you, because I think it impacts upon what it is you are called upon to do with this matter, that the likelihood of such agreements in the future has been severely diminished. I cannot enter into any agreement on agreed facts without the consent of my client. That can't happen. The second thing that the preamble of the document told us was this: That with regard to the Sanski Most phase of the case, the Trial Chamber had compiled such a list of facts itself. Numerous questions rise from that immediately: How did the Chamber arrive at this list; from what source did the Chamber compile these alleged facts; what criteria did the Trial Chamber use in including some facts and eliminating others; how could the Trial Chamber have gotten so many of the alleged facts completely wrong; have they not been listening to the evidence in this case; how could the Trial Chamber include facts as subject to agreement that have been disputed long and loud from the first day of this case. Is this list an expression by the Trial Chamber that, after serious consideration, it believes these to be facts that the Defence could not reasonably challenge; what price will the defendant pay if the defendant refuses to agree to the Chamber's suggestions. All these are questions directly related to the question of whether this is a fair trial by an impartial Tribunal. Although I accept that the three Judges were completely unaware of this document, modified this morning, Your Honour, by what you learned in your consultation with Judge Agius, the Judges permitted this to happen either by action or inaction. It is of no particular import, it seems, by whom this document was authored. It came from Chambers, from persons who have impact on the thinking of the Judges, who advise the Judges and consult with them on both legal and factual matters. As lead counsel in this case, I could not absolve myself of responsibility for a document filed with the Trial Chamber by explaining that I had not seen it before it was filed; nor should I be able to. While I accept that the Trial Chamber did not know of the document, the Trial Chamber must accept responsibility for it. I did not hear that in the statement of Judge Agius yesterday. In fact, what the Judge said was this: "The three Judges wish to state that the motion is obviously based on a misconception, in that none of us, the three Judges in this trial, had anything to do with the compilation, let alone the drafting, of the list of possible agreed facts for consideration." I could compare that statement with the minutes that you gave us this morning, Your Honour. I will leave that to you. I must ask how this could have happened if the Judges had nothing to do with it, although I have learned this morning that the President of the Court did have something to do with it. Finally, the author of this document and those responsibility for distributing it obviously did not think for even a fleeting moment about the impact such a document would have on the accused in this case. Your Honour has spoken this morning correctly about part of the mission of this Tribunal being a peace-keeping mission. You know that this Tribunal has been frequently criticised both in the Serbian press and in other non-Serbian highly regarded publications for being decidedly anti-Serb. The numbers are difficult to explain. The award of provisional release is difficult to explain in any other terms. To come forward with a document that on its face would suggest to an already suspicious accused that the Chamber had made conclusions regarding the Sanski Most facts after hearing only two hours of testimony from one witness is shocking in its complete naivete. I hate to the say this, but I must speak the truth: This document will haunt this case from now on. It will never be forgotten. It will always be seen by the accused as a stark indication that they are not receiving, and will not receive, a fair trial. That is an unfortunately reality. Nothing we do here today or in the coming days can change that unfortunately reality. The perception of this Tribunal by the public will change in some perceptible degree. That change has already begun. It seems to me that this Tribunal now has an obligation to show the world, to show these accused, that the concern for peace-keeping and peace-making and fairness and impartiality is a real one. What I believe as counsel, what I believe myself, Your Honour, as counsel, regarding the partiality or impartiality of this Trial Chamber as presently constituted is of little moment at this stage. There has clearly been an impropriety. Its impact on the accused has been profound. No amount of explanation about how it was a mistake, a misunderstanding, or that the Chamber did not know of it, will remove it and its stain from this case. I want to for just a moment make an additional statement that is not part of our agreed joint statement, because I think it is appropriate. The minutes of the meeting that you held with the Judges, I said at the beginning, confirmed some suspicions that I had. It appears from those minutes that Judges Janu and Taya had no knowledge whatsoever of any of the matters contained in this motion until sometime yesterday, when they were handed their copies of the motion. I think that is very unfortunate, and had I known that, they of course would not have been included in this motion. In the process of disposing of this motion, it may very well be the appropriate disposition that those Judges be treated differently than the presiding Judge who was aware of what was happening. I say that only for myself and my own client, Your Honour. Your Honour has invited me to discuss the law. I have not prepared myself to do that. I am somewhat familiar with prior matters regarding these issues as they have gone on in this Chamber because I have written on them and because I was somewhat intimately involved in the evidence to disqualify Judge Odio Benito. I think I can only say this: That with regard to the issue of Judge Odio Benito, it was a matter that arose very, very, very deeply into that trial and a matter in which no showing was made, or could have been made, of actual or real impartiality on the part of that Judge. With regard to the matter that arose in the Furundzija case, where an attempt was made to disqualify Judge Mumba, I believe the Chamber was correct in the sense that mere membership on a United Nations commission regarding the status of women could not reasonably be seen as a basis for the disqualification of a Judge. There was no allegation of any kind made against Judge Mumba that impacted her specific impartiality regarding specific issues in the Furundzija case. So I think these cases that have been previously dealt with by Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this Tribunal really shed very little light beyond some sort of general principles as to how the matter before Your Honour now should be treated. It seems to me that this case is at an early enough stage that there may be a fairly simple solution to the problem. And I will suggest that solution if I am asked to, but I think it is not my place to do that unless asked. I appreciate being given the opportunity to address Your Honour about this. I need to try to make clear to you that this was not something that I think was filed irresponsibly or precipitously. I think it is a very, very serious matter that goes to the very heart of what goes on in this Tribunal. And I hope it will be taken as seriously as it is intended to be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Madam Fauveau-Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I entirely support what has been said by Mr. Ackerman as far as Judges Janu and Taya are concerned and, in any case, it was a joint declaration. However, I should like to add the following. The list of facts that has been given to us shows and demonstrates profound knowledge of the facts which took place in Sanski Most. I am not saying that these facts are correct or incorrect, however, the fact that such a list has been composed demonstrates that the author of the list has a certain opinion regarding the events which occurred in the municipality of Sanski Most. The knowledge of these facts was not obtained, however, in the courtroom. Such a knowledge was obtained elsewhere. Rule 15(A), Rules of Procedure and Evidence provides as follows: "A Judge may not sit on a trial or appeal in any case in which the Judge has a personal interest or concerning which the Judge has or has had any association which might affect his or her impartiality." I consider that the fact that an individual who -- a staff member who belongs to a Chamber has knowledge of the facts demonstrates that he has some association with this case. I have also seen the minutes of the meeting which have just been given to us. In point 14, it seems that Judge Agius was not agreeable to certain facts which are contained in the list which has been given to us. Let me draw your attention to the fact that the list in question contains, apart from the facts that Judge Agius conceded that should not have been incorporated in the list, it contains the destruction of the mosque in Kukavica, which is part a part of the allegations in the indictment. The list also includes the transport of the dead to the Manjaca camp from Krings, which is also not contained in the indictment. It also contains the death of the individuals during the transport from the Sanski Most sports hall to Manjaca, a fact which is also not included in the indictment. I don't know how the author of this list was able to obtain such knowledge. I do not intend to instigate an inquiry into the issue. It does not fall within my competence. I do not see how the serious facts such as the death of 18 people, 20 people, and the destruction of the mosque, the facts which are not contained in the indictment, can be found on this list. And now we are asked to agree to these facts. If the author of the list had the knowledge of these facts, if he was able, he or she was able to obtain such knowledge from the statements of the witnesses of Sanski Most municipality, it is inappropriate before this Chamber that the Chamber should reach conclusions, should make findings on the basis of the statement of witnesses who have not been heard by the Chamber. It is also inappropriate to consider a statement of a witness to be truthful without having heard this witness and without having given the opportunity to the witness to cross-examine -- the opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness. At any rate, it is inappropriate for a Chamber, be it a Judge or a member of the Chamber, to ask from us to recognise the facts, to agree to the facts which are not contained in the indictment. If it is in the interest -- if the purpose is to expedite the proceedings and the Chamber considers there should be no hearing on such facts, then they should have asked the Prosecutor not to call evidence concerning the facts which were not contained in the indictment, and not to ask the accused to agree to such facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Merci. Before I give the floor to Office of the Prosecutor to be very precise on the limits of the motion before us, is it my correct understanding that the Defence counsels' intent to withdraw the motion as regards Judge Janu and Judge Taya?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Based upon your conversations with them, it is clear that they had absolutely nothing to do with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. And then we can have the contribution of the Office of the Prosecutor, limited to the remaining part of the issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I am sorry. I had told Judge Agius yesterday that I would tell you straightaway today that we also have no objection to the Trial Chamber as presently constituted continuing to hear this case during the pendency of this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: : This was already part of my order yesterday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to deal first of all, because it is the simplest, with what Ms. Fauveau has just said about the facts that were put into this document. She said, and I have said this before to her, that it doesn't appear in the indictment the Krings issue. We have always made it clear that what was put into the indictment was not all the incidents about which we were going to lead evidence, because there were so many of them. We specified the major incidents at the request of Judge Hunt. It was clear, not only from the evidence but from the pre-trial brief, and we have turned it up and it is in the part that deals with Sanski Most, where we make it absolutely clear that we are going to be leading the evidence about that. And I should imagine, as that is a public file document with the Chamber, that that is where these facts were taken from. Can I come back to the very real issue in this case. I attempted yesterday, in a lengthy explanation, really for the benefit of the accused, what such a document was intended to achieve. And I don't propose to go through it again because they had me say this yesterday. Mr. Ackerman has said, as he said yesterday and in the conference that was held with Mr. Harmon - with Mr. Von Hebel, I'm sorry - that everyone should consider the impact on the accused. Your Honour, I have to say that I am surprised that counsel of the experience of Mr. Ackerman and Ms. Fauveau, who are both trusted by their clients - because there has been a number of discussions about representation during the course of this trial - were unable to explain to their clients what has been so obvious right from the beginning and is obvious to both Defence counsel: First, that this was not, clearly, at no stage, any expression of any bias or belief by the Trial Chamber that these facts that were set out, and I quote, "for consideration, to consider the facts for discussion," was any type of expression of their finding of fact. In addition to which, Mr. Ackerman told Your Honour that this was after hearing two hours of evidence. At the time that this list was handed out to counsel, not one word of evidence in respect of Sanski Most had been heard because the witness who is now testifying had not yet started to testify. And so clearly that cannot be right, and that is why I say that I am surprised that this was not explained to the two accused properly by their own counsel. It is clear that these facts were written for consideration. That is repeated again. And it is equally clear that what the Chamber through its legal officers was attempting to do, as has been made clear in numerous discussions both before Judge Hunt and the Trial Chamber as it is now constituted, or Judge Agius when he was acting as Pre-Trial Judge, that in a case which involves the superior responsibility of the accused where, because they have no personal knowledge or evidence to contradict evidence of crimes in which it is not alleged they personally took part, in order to try and reduce the trial to manageable proportions, which is in the interest of the accused, as I explained yesterday, it is possible and it is universal, I think, in all jurisdictions that facts which are not disputed do not specifically have to be proved by the calling of evidence. Now, what happened, and it is clear to everyone and Defence counsel have made it clear that they accept it, is that part of the staff or someone on the staff prepared a set of facts for consideration arising from what was said in the pre-trial brief, which they thought it was possible to discuss and see if their agreement to be reached. They put down facts clearly on which, had they known, had they followed the progress of events for the last two and-a-half years, were never likely to be agreed, namely, for example, that General Talic accepted that he was a member of the ARK Crisis Staff. Even if it was never likely to be agreed, what is the problem with saying, however politely or impolitely it is put, of course we can't agree that that is a matter which is in dispute. It is the Prosecution's submission that regrettably, and maybe for reasons that are somewhat outside this, the way this motion is put, this matter has been blown up out of all proportion. Your Honour, it would seem to the international community that one of the major efforts that should be achieved by Judges of this Tribunal is that the trial should be kept manageable, be dealt with expeditiously, and that people who are awaiting trial in this Tribunal - if the press are right, more are likely to arrive - should be able to stand trial as soon as is proper within the interest of justice. And there is nothing wrong with the preparation of such facts for discussion. It is open at any stage for the Defence to say we will not or we cannot agree these particular facts. But there has already been agreement reached in respect of a particular witness who was called some fortnight ago now, where both counsel got up in terms and said that they were not going to dispute the killing, that this witness had been called to testify about. And there was discussion that there had been, perhaps we can say it was a misunderstanding by the Prosecution, but we had not understood that it was unnecessary to call this witness and, indeed, there was discussion about whether or not in future the Defence could make it absolutely clear, in advance, what evidence they were not disputing from particular witnesses. So I have to say Your Honours, again, that I find it a little difficult to understand why these two Defence counsel were unable to explain to their clients how this document had been drafted when it jumped out at everyone. Now, Your Honour, I am going to turn to the law. I am a little surprised that Mr. Ackerman wasn't prepared because I raised it with him yesterday that there was authority that I proposed to refer to. Before I do that, Your Honour, I have no doubt that Your Honour will be impressed by what I can only call an inter alia approach taken by Mr. Ackerman, namely, that this trial will be prolonged because it is unlikely that he will be able to enter into any agreement on any facts in the light of this, or that nothing about this document can be forgotten. These are, I imagine, statements made for public consumption but in our submission do not assist on the criteria that Your Honour has to apply, now reduced to the question of Judge Agius remaining on this trial. Your Honour, if one starts with the two Rules that Your Honours have already referred to, Rule 15, "A Judge may not sit on a trial or appeal in any case in which the Judge has a personal interest," that doesn't seem to be the matter that is raised, "or concerning which the Judge has or has had any association which might affect his or her impartiality," and I imagine, although it's not very clearly expressed in the motion, that it is based on that. And then Rule 15(B), the application. Your Honour, this matter has been considered on our researches in this Tribunal on three separate occasions. I don't know whether Your Honours has been given or has already got a copy of a decision in the Prosecutor versus Delalic and others on the 25th of October, 1999. It was a decision of the Bureau. We can hand, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour has it. I am grateful.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the 21st of July, the case of the Prosecutor against Furundzija, which was an Appeals Chamber decision and where there was a consideration of all the authorities and then, finally, on the 18th of May last year -- I'm sorry, 2000, so two years ago nearly, in this particular case, Brdjanin and Talic. Does Your Honour have a copy of all three? I am grateful. Your Honour, if one starts with what is generally known as the Celebici case and that decision, Delalic and others, this was a motion that Judge Odio Benito should be disqualified from presiding on the basis that she had been appointed the Vice President of Costa Rica. And it was a discussion of the applicable law which began at page 5, paragraph 6: The issue of the grounds of disqualification of a Judge from sitting in a particular case. And they then quoted the Statute in the following paragraphs. Your Honour, I am going to go straight to paragraph 10, where they dealt with the two issues. There may be some overlap between the two issues, that is to say whether the Judge is disqualified for reasons of the two matters set out in Rule 15. This may happen when a party to a trial or appellate proceedings claims that the fact that the Judge is sitting in that case has engaged in political, administrative or professional activities which entails the consequence that this Judge has a personal interest in the case or has some association with the case causing the Judge to be biased and hence to lack the required impartiality. Clearly, in this case, the party raising the issue of disqualification must show that the alleged incompatibilities with the judicial function are such as to bring about a lack of impartiality in the case at issue. In other words, that party must show a link between the activity allegedly incompatible with the judicial function and the particular case at issue. It would not be sufficient for that party to claim merely that the Judge in question is exercising a political, administrative or professional activity incompatible with his or her judicial functions. And, in fact, the Judges ruled that the defendants, the accused in this case, had failed to demonstrate that. But I emphasise that the burden lies squarely on the applicant to show that there is good reason why a Judge should not continue to sit. Your Honour, if one turns to the case of Furundzija, decided by the Appeals Chamber on the 21st of July, 2000. This related again to Judge Mumba, who seems to be somewhat unfortunate as far as these motions are concerned. This was, as Mr. Ackerman has rightly stated, the question of whether her activities in a particular woman's organisation disqualified her. If one goes straight to paragraph 177, which dealt with the Article 13 of the Statute, providing that the Judges of the International Tribunal shall be persons of high moral character, impartiality and integrity. Going then on to 55, I think, but paragraph 179: "Interpretation of the fundamental human right of an accused person to be tried by an impartial tribunal is carried out by considering situations in which it is alleged that a Judge is not or cannot be impartial and therefore should be disqualified from sitting on a particular case. A two-pronged approach appears to have developed. Although interpretation on a national or regional level is not uniform, as a general rule, courts will find that a judge might not bring an impartial and unprejudiced mind to a case if there is proof of actual bias or of an appearance of bias." And in fact, of course, it was actually decided after the Talic decision because that comes straight from the Talic decision, so I should have dealt with that one first. Your Honour, they then went on to say, "The appellant acknowledges that he makes no claim that Judge Mumba was actually biased." And indeed, as I understand it, neither accused counsel alleges that Judge Agius is biased. What is suggested is that by the fact of his knowledge that something like this document was to be handed to us, he has given some kind of indication of bias, and as I have already said, any common sense reading shows this just cannot be so. Your Honour, if one goes in the Furundzija judgment to paragraph 182: "In considering subjective impartiality, the Court has repeatedly declared that the personal impartiality of a Judge must be presumed until there is proof to the contrary. In relation to the objective test, the Court has found that this requires that a Tribunal is not only genuinely impartial, but also appears to be impartial. Even if there is no suggestion of actual bias, where appearances may give rise to doubts about impartiality, the Court has found that this alone may amount to an inadmissible jeopardy of the confidence which the Court must inspire in a democratic society. The Court considers that it must determine whether or not there are ascertainable facts which may raise doubt as to impartiality. In doing so, it has found that in deciding," and the quote is given, and this comes from a human rights case called Housechild, I think, something like Housechilde, "whether in a given case there is legitimate reason to fear that a particular Judge lacks impartiality, the standpoint of the accused is important, but not decisive. What is decisive is whether this fear can be held objectively justified. Thus one must ascertain, apart from whether a Judge has shown actual bias, whether one can apprehend an appearance of bias." Your Honour, in our submission, this is, as it were, squarely on all fours. Mr. Ackerman says that the two accused cannot understand this. I have already dealt with the inability to fully comprehend why experienced counsel couldn't explain this. But in any event, having heard discussed in open court in front of them - and digressing for a moment, Your Honour, that is why we thought it important to have this hearing so that the accused can be present. Having heard the discussion, having heard what is being said, Your Honours, we submit that any fears that they may have had must be allayed by what they have heard discussed and what Your Honours -- what Your Honour has told them. Your Honour, the discussion then went on to look at the various Rules arising from the various jurisdictions: From the United Kingdom, real danger of bias rather than a real likelihood, finding it is unnecessary in formulating the appropriate test to require that the Court should look at the matter through the eyes of a reasonable man because the Court has first to ascertain the relevant circumstances from the available evidence, knowledge of which would not necessarily be available to an observer in Court at the relevant time. And it goes on to say that other common law jurisdictions have rejected this test as being too strict. And then Webb and the South African Rugby Football Union case, again, which was Human Rights case, I think, say that -- use the reasonable person as the arbiter of bias, investing him with the requisite knowledge of the circumstances before an assessment as to impartiality can be made. I'm sorry, it was the Supreme Court of South Africa that dealt with the football case. They dealt with the Australian authorities. And then at paragraph 188, the German code of criminal procedure, which I wouldn't have the temerity to address Your Honour on. Finally, the standard to be applied by the Appeals Chamber which is at paragraph 189 onwards, "Having consulted this jurisprudence, the Appeals Chamber finds that there a general rule that a Judge should not only be subjectively free from bias, but also that there should be nothing in the surrounding circumstances which objectively gives rise to an appearance of bias. On this basis, the Appeals Chamber considers that following principle should be directed interpreting and implying the impartiality requirement of the Statute. A Judge is not impartial if it is shown that actual bias exists. No such bias has been shown or is suggested. B, there is an unacceptable appearance of bias if, one, a Judge is a party to the case or has a financial or proprietary interest in the outcome of a case or if the Judges decision would lead to the promotion of a cause in which he or she is involved together with one of the parties. Under these circumstances, a Judge's disqualification from the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. case is automatic. Or, two, the circumstances would lead a reasonable observer, properly informed, to reasonably apprehend bias. In terms of the second branch of the second principle, the Appeals Chamber adopts the approach that the reasonable person must be an informed person with knowledge of all the relevant circumstance including the traditions of integrity and impartiality that form a part of the background and apprised also of the fact that impartiality is one of the duties that Judges swear to uphold. Your Honour, the reasonable observer informed of the facts that in an effort to manage a long and complex, heavily documented, weighty trial, the Presiding Judge attempted to find some method through the legal officer whereby the parties could discuss and reach agreement on certain facts in the case, but through some perhaps not particularly good draftsmanship which it might be said, I suppose, that the Judge to that limited extent, perhaps, should have exercised the right to correct, attempted to draft matters for discussion could in any way be said to be not impartial or biased towards the accused. And I should add, as I said yesterday, Judge Agius, when he was discussing this in one of the earlier conferences, said that in no way would any agreement on facts that need not -- that might not be in issue in any way suggest the guilt or any admission of culpability by the accused. Your Honour, we submit -- and, Your Honour, I think that is the test because the rest deals with the particular application to Judge Mumba. Your Honour, unless Your Honour would like me to go through the Brdjanin and Talic decision, in fact, I think most of the principles were covered by this. Your Honours, our submission is a very simple one and I said it before and I will say it again. Not only has no bias been alleged or demonstrated, but on the facts of this case, they cannot be said to be any impression given that there could be bias or anything to take away from the principal that justice must not only be done but be seen to be done. Your Honour, unless there is any other aspect that you would like me to address you on, those are our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not on the moment, but thank you. I should give the opportunity for an answer of course to the Defence counsel. Please understand that I can't go into any substantive points. May I only add two words I still have in my mind from the contributions of the parties. First of all, the word proportionality should be one main factor of that what is contributed here. And as I said before, having been involved myself as a Defence counsel in situations in that you are right now, having submitted myself motions on the disqualification on Judges, I must admit that to a certain extent I can understand your point. That doesn't mean that I share your view. But please one thing I wanted to ask you, you said this document this will never be forgotten. I believe in life and in courtroom that is a part of life. We should never proceed with the idea something will never be forgotten, something will never be forgiven. We are all human beings making possibly the one or other mistakes. But please I appreciate to hear your additional comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have clearly pointed out that that point needs some clarification, Your Honour, and I will give it to you. What I mean when I say to you, "that document will never be forgotten," I look back at the Celebici case which started, I believe, in the spring of 1998 and the case is still going on. I see this case still going on perhaps in the Appeal Chamber four or five years from now, and this document remaining a part of the issues in the case throughout that entire period. There is no way for me to predict what this document will mean outside this trial -- this Tribunal. I don't know. So when I say it will not be forgotten, I say it will affect and haunt this case throughout its life. I do want to comment if you will permit me just very briefly on a couple of things Ms. Korner said to you. She first said that the International Community is interested in trials being held here in a manageable and expeditious way. And I agree with that. But that is a secondary consideration. The first consideration of the International Community is that the trials here be fair and impartial and be seen to be fair and impartial. It is not enough just that justice be done, but justice must be seen to be done. I think this case changed rather dramatically this morning. What Ms. Korner said to you was the case until this morning about the factual basis for our motion, this is not easy for me. Yesterday, in open court, Judge Agius said, "None of us, the three Judges in this trial, had anything to do with the compilation, let alone the drafting of the list of possible agreed facts for consideration." This morning, as a result of your meeting with the Judges, we learned that Judge Agius instructed the staff to consult with parties through this pre-municipality meeting and try to identify with the parties facts on which they could possibly agree. Paragraph 13, Judge Agius was provided a memo on the pre-municipality meeting one day before that meeting. That memo included also a possible list of agreed facts that was not identical to the one distributed to the parties inter alia. The heading of the document did not appear in the memo provided to Judge Agius. Although it is a bit ambiguous, Your Honour, it appears that the facts that appeared in the memo distributed to us were in the memo received by Judge Agius and it was only the heading, the preamble to the document, that was not there. I believe and I suggest to you that the things Judge Agius has told you in your meeting with him differ rather significantly from what he told us in open court yesterday. And I think that raises additional concerns that Your Honour needs to address. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am quite surprised that Ms. Korner tells us what is the problem to say that we do not agree that General Talic was a member of the Crisis Staff. In fact, I wouldn't have had this problem if this was coming from the Prosecutor, but I do know that the Prosecutor would never have asked this question. Because however paradoxical it sounds, the Prosecutor looks at our motions and reads them and listens to us. But this person who wrote this has never read any of our conclusions, any of our lists, has not read anything or has not been listening to us during the hearings, and this is a great worry to us. As far as the facts that are concerned that are not in the indictment but are linked to the trial, in the pre-trial brief, I would like to say two things. The first thing is that this, the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal, in the Kupreskic case, said clearly that that person can only be tried for the facts that are alleged in the indictment. And another remark concerns exactly the impartiality. If a person who comes from the Chamber could have taken this as truth without giving us the possibility to contradict it, the content of the Prosecution pre-trial brief, this is clearly a very clear signal of partiality, of bias.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before coming to a break, I want to ask the Defence counsels to be prepared to address also the point made by the Office of the Prosecutor whether or not a possible negligence or omission can amount to a reason of disqualification, can amount to a Judge's being biased. This may be -- I can't at this point in time decide what will be the actual and most important issues, but this may one question and therefore I would ask you to address this as well. And in addition, because it was said in Furundzija that the standpoint of the accused is not decisive, but is important. I invite also the accused themselves to speak to the court if they so want. And you may discuss this issue during the break with your clients. We will adjourn and resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming a 11.30 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We come back to the very serious issue before us, and once again before giving you the floor, I want to emphasise that we have to be aware of the tests to be applied and this is first of all whether in a given case there is legitimate reason to fear that a particular judge lacks impartiality. The standpoint of the accused is important, but not decisive. What is decisive is whether this fear can be held objectively justified. And therefore let me briefly address this question once more. I know this is only part and only one element of the entire issue, but please understand that I have learned from a point of view of a Defence counsel, it is sometimes better to know what is in the Judge's head instead of being surprised later on the outcome of a decision. I regard this is a part of the right to be heard. And therefore, as I said before, having compared once again yesterday's statements and the minutes of today, one could say that indeed Judge Agius was aware that, in quotation marks, "something" should be presented to the parties on agreed facts, but it remains he never saw the incriminative document. Isn't it right that the possible problem comes down to the question, how is it possible that this incriminated document came into the hands of the parties? Shouldn't it be cross-checked before by the presiding Judge? Isn't this more or less - I have to be cautious myself - negligence or an omission? Can this really amount to being biased? Shouldn't it also be taken into account that reading very carefully yesterday's statement and the statement of today, being aware of his duty to certain kind of loyalty against the staff, though having not read the incriminated document, clearly dissociated himself from this document? I would appreciate if you would comment on these additional points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The first thing I think, Your Honour, is you have made it clear that from your own experience you have some understanding of the difficulty that I face with regard to dealing with this situation and I appreciate that very much. It is true, of course, that one can read the statement of Judge Agius yesterday as a statement of loyalty, not just to the staff, but to the other two Judges who obviously were completely taken aback and surprised by receiving the motion yesterday and the document attached to it. On the other hand, Your Honour, you must also recognise that this was not a private statement made by the Judge, but a public statement made by the Judge regarding his own knowledge and participation with regard to this document. And it certainly does differ from what he has told you a day later. Your question about can negligence ever form the basis for disqualification, I don't know that any court in the world has ever answered that question. It is an important question and an interesting question. I think that the presiding Judge of a Trial Chamber must be viewed very much like the captain of the ship. It may be that it was a mistake for the person manning the machine-gun to fire on the lifeboat. And it may be that the captain of the ship neither knew that would happen nor directed that it happen, but the perception of the people in the lifeboat is the same. And I think that is the point here. Judge Agius is captain of that ship and it happened on his watch and should not have, and he admits that it should not have happened. The fact that it did changed the face of this case. Now, whether it changed the face of this case to such an extent that something must be done about it is a matter that is in, what I believe to be, your very capable hands, Your Honour. We are, to continue the naval analysis, sailing in uncharted waters to some extent. I think we should sail carefully. And I hope that I am doing that, and I have every confidence that you will. Before the break you suggested that we consult with our clients to see if they wanted to address you regarding this matter. I have done that. I think Mr. Brdjanin would like to make a very brief statement to you. And if I have not answered your question as completely as you would like, please let me know and I will try to do better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madame Fauveau. Please, first, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: I fully support what my colleague Mr. Ackerman has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before coming to the statements of the accused, I once more want to point out what are, in a comparative international approach, first of all, the tests applied. And the tests applied, they all, first of all, quote: "That on the basis of the additional facts provided, that is concreto the statement yesterday, the minutes of today, that on the basis of the additional facts provided, can a responsible observer, an objective or neutral layman and/or accused not learned in the legal sciences, still believe in the impartiality of a Judge?" This is a question and I would appreciate to get an answer from Mr. Brdjanin and General Talic, not before I have, as it is usual, to tell them, that it is of course your right to remain silent, but you have to be aware that every word in the courtroom may be used as evidence, even as evidence against you. So it is only your right to speak. If you so want, Mr. Brdjanin, please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time that I am witnessing a trial and it happens to be my trial. I have had, of course, opportunity to see it on TV and on film. As you have indicated, it is a rather technical matter for me, but if I may, I should like to say the following: The conclusions and the findings reached must be true. With my counsel, as it was who was appointed two years ago, I discussed everything and I have always been quite satisfied. However, once this trial started, I have had certain reasons for doubt. Not regarding the counsel, but the fairness of the trial. I would like -- I wish I were mistaken, but let me take this example. Let me explain to you what happened with the document. When it arrive yesterday, I said, "Mr. Ackerman, that it seems that my doubts were not fully and justified." I know that this can be used against me, but I have to say that it was my impression, my impression. I have to emphasise that what I learned from films is actually true, that the Judges do not only want to establish the truth. I accept that -- I expect that the Judges place the utmost importance on the truth, regardless of what the Prosecutor say. My first counsel, my co-counsel was thrown out because of certain doubts, certain allegations, that he was not telling the truth, then I can go on with many such examples, but as I said, I am a lay person when it comes to these matters. It all comes down to the fact that I do not think, I do not believe that I will receive a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, what Mr. Brdjanin is saying to you is not being translated appropriately.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If Mr. Brdjanin could be kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Probably the problem can be resolved --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have problems following Mr. Brdjanin. If he could please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If Mr. Brdjanin is slowing a little bit down, but also the Judges can understand him or that I can understand you in a language I understand. If you could slow down. Please repeat your last sentences. It was on the first counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN
utterances.text: I have lived to see my co-counsel eliminated. To see my second investigator with a large amount of experience was not appointed to be another co-counsel, and now we are looking for a third solution. I have lived to see many things that have increased my doubts in the fairness of the trial and that in the doubt of my right to a fair trial. Now, that is what I wanted to demonstrate here and that is why I believe -- I agree with Mr. Ackerman what he just said, but I would like to emphasise again, that throughout this time it was Mr. Ackerman who was telling me that I was not right to have these doubts, but now this document has proved that I have been right, that I could not just come to the trial quietly and expect to have this trial before the International Tribunal, which is open and public. I cannot skip this and so I will finish. I believe -- I believe that in this case, in our case, there will be more protected witnesses than in other cases. All of this, in my mother submission, is not legally based but all this has brought to my opinion, to my viewpoint, and Mr. Ackerman has pointed out exactly what I think, and I would like to -- I would have preferred if this hadn't happened, and if I hadn't had the opportunity to come and to reach such conclusions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. General Talic, do you want to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED TALIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not wish to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, as representative of -- Defence counsel of General Talic, I would like to say, if we didn't have doubts on the impartiality of the Chamber, we would not have submitted this motion. The problem is not how this document came into our hands, and it arrived into our hands in a very simple manner: It came directly from the Chamber. It was communicated to us personally by one of the legal officers of the Chamber. But that is not important. What is important is how such a document could have been written. This document speaks for itself. This document is irrefutable proof, and it now has become public, of the partiality of one of the Judges who is sitting on the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Contributions from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I am really sorry to have to say this, but I think particularly this last contribution from Madame Fauveau is a deliberate refusal to listen to the explanations that have been given by the Judges and by everyone. Your Honour, if I may respectfully say this, it seems to me that what concerns Mr. Brdjanin is not this particular document but the fact that co-counsel in this case has been suspended and that, as I say, I imagined, on behalf of the Prosecutor, that there was more to this than met the eye. The accused has already expressed his anxiety at an investigation that has been launched and is being carried out by the Registry into certain aspects of co-counsel's behaviour. And it seems to us that effectively he hasn't dealt with whether he now understands the situation now that it has been explained to him. And in response to Your Honour's questions to Defence counsel as to whether negligence, if it is negligence, can amount to a basis for disqualification, Your Honours, our submission is, no, not on the authorities, not on the clear wording of the Statute and the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before concluding, I want to point out that, of course, we have to remain in the framework of proportionality and I was interested on the statements of the two accused, and what I heard from Mr. Brdjanin was, first of all, the fear of impartiality or partiality - better - of the entire proceedings, but nothing precisely on the alleged partiality of Judge Agius, and as regards the comments of -- I say this once again to give you another possibility if you so want to add something. The contribution Madame Fauveau was, to put it very frank, on the partiality of a document but not of a Judge, and I know this is a very difficult situation and of course everybody, and I emphasise "everybody" in the entire Tribunal, would have appreciated if this document never had appeared. It's evidently the expression of the enthusiasm of the one -- I didn't investigate it -- of the one or other member of the staff. But please correct me. The basis before me does not prove that Judge Agius was aware and authorised the publication of this unfortunate document, I must say. In concluding already, at university, and it was a very good guidance throughout my life - at that time I was a defence counsel - my highly estimated professor always told me, it is good to warn judges that they may be biased, that they may give the impression to be biased and to threaten with a motion on disqualification, and if there is an additional necessity, file such a motion, but never let it be decided. And I believe there is some truth in it because we all are, and should be, interested that we have also internal peace in courtroom. And therefore my serious question is to the Defence counsels: On the basis what you have seen yesterday and today and also take into account, though not being responsible for this, but acting on behalf of the entire Tribunal, take -- please take my apologies what has happened here with this unfortunate document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think you just asked me if I accept your apologies. And, of course, I do. I accept your apologies with what happened with the document. It should not have happened. We both agree with that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So there is no intention at all, I understand, to withdraw the motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I cannot withdraw the motion. I absolutely cannot. This motion should be granted. In the interest of the future of this case and justice, it should be granted. There is a simple way to deal with this and I'd be happy to tell you what it is, in my mind, and I have told you that before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the parties will as soon as possible receive a decision in writing, first of all, as you know whether or not to transfer the case to the Bureau or not. Unfortunately, I can't indicate today when this will be, but as I said already in my decision yesterday, please continue, first of all in the interest of justice, and in the interest of the witness brought to The Hague with the case to be heard this afternoon and in the following days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just in case Your Honour wasn't aware, the Brdjanin and Talic case is not sitting at all next week. So maybe that will give Your Honour the opportunity to deliver a judgment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Whenever it will come out. Until then, the hearing may continue as it was scheduled. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: adjourned at 12.00 p.m.
